newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-CRASH ENDS ERTL'S CHAMPIONSHIP HOPES.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-CRASH ENDS ERTL'S CHAMPIONSHIP HOPES.

text.p: Germany's Martina Ertl, an Olympic giant slalom silver medallist, had her world championship hopes ended on Thursday by a crash in training for a World Cup Alpine skiing downhill.
The fall overshadowed an otherwise uneventful day in which the sun replaced the fog and snow that had forced the cancellation of Tuesday's and Wednesday's training.

Russian Warwara Zelenskaja, looking for her second career win, set the day's fastest time of one minute 31.24 seconds in her second run down the Olimpia delle Tofane piste ahead of Switzerland's on-form Heidi Zurbriggen in 1:31.29.
Two runs were scheduled to make up for the ones lost to the weather earlier in the week.

Sweden's overall World Cup leader Pernilla Wiberg, second in a downhill here last year and closing in on a first win in the discipline, was fastest in the opening session, 0.44 seconds ahead of Zelenskaya's 1:32.46.
The Swede clocked 1:32.02 before Ertl crashed. She was fourth fastest in a second run as some racers cut more than a second off their initial times on the quick piste.
Isolde Kostner, one of the winners of last year's two downhills, was third fastest despite slowing up deliberately.
Ertl, the women's World Cup giant slalom champion, injured ligaments in her left knee in her fall.
It was the same knee that she injured in October, forcing her out for a month, and team sources saw little hope of her racing again this season.
"She has gone to Munich now and there the doctor will make a diagnosis," said team mate Katja Seizinger, who beat Ertl into second place in last year's overall World Cup.
The Sestriere world championships start in 10 days time.
The German won a giant bronze medal at the 1996 Sierra Nevada championships and in the 1993 championships.
Cortina hosts a downhill on Friday, followed by a super-G on Saturday and a giant slalom on Sunday.
The downhill will be the fourth of a season disrupted by bad weather and the penultimate before the championships.
However, Cortina should be the first 'real' downhill of the women's season to be held in Europe.
A race held in Bad Kleinkircheim, Austria, on January 11 was disrupted by fog with the result declared before some late starters had been able to get on the piste.
Another downhill in the resort was cancelled while the December Crans Montana downhill was also called off.

Some skiers, notably downhill World Cup leader Seizinger, who is Wiberg's main rival for the overall title, were critical of a race schedule which has three downhills planned for Japan and the United States after Sestriere.

"I think it's a problem. There are so many downhills after the championships and there's no time to make them up if there are any problems in Japan," said Seizinger, well aware that Wiberg is stronger in the technical disciplines.
"I think it's stupid," the German said of a schedule that has given downhillers little action before Sestriere.
"Hopefully we can race here tomorrow and perhaps also next week in Laax and then that should be enough.
"If there's any problem at the end of the season with the weather then the downhills are gone, we can't repeat them any more. That's a problem and a disadvantage."
Canada's Kate Pace Lindsay echoed her words.
"It's been terrible," she said. "It's been really hard to get something going and to keep positive all the time when day after day it's cancelled."
